Recall the human system: what holds our main airway open, how many tracheas do we have, and where exactly does gas exchange into blood happen?
walkthrough:
**See what the insect does**

Look at the labels. Tracheae branch into tiny tracheoles that lie right next to respiring body cells. Gas exchange happens directly across the tracheole wall into the cell. There is no blood system in between.

**Recall what humans do differently**

In humans, air travels down one single trachea, then bronchi, bronchioles, to the alveoli. Gas exchange happens only at the alveoli into capillaries, then blood carries gases to body cells. Airways themselves do not supply cells directly.

**Check each statement**

Statement 1 is true because direct delivery to cells is unique to insects. Statement 2 is true because insects use chitin spirals (taenidia) to hold tracheae open, while humans use C-shaped cartilage rings in the trachea, not chitin. Statement 3 is true because insects have a branching network of many tracheae from many spiracles, while humans have only one trachea. All three are correct, so the answer is A.

options.A: Correct. All three statements are true differences. Insects exchange directly to cells, use chitin, and have many tracheae, while humans do not.
options.B: Incomplete. Statements 1 and 2 are correct, but statement 3 is also correct so this option misses one true difference.
options.C: Incomplete. Statements 2 and 3 are correct, but statement 1 is also correct because humans never exchange gases directly from airways to body cells.
options.D: Incomplete. Statement 3 alone is correct, but statements 1 and 2 are also correct differences, so this misses two points.
